# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Movies where reality slowly stops making sense, but nobody explains why

**Score:** 230
**Body:** I’m looking for movies that begin in a relatively recognizable reality, but little by little **the normal rules seem to stop working**.

Not necessarily movies with a big twist or a final explanation. Actually, I prefer when the characters themselves gradually accept increasingly bizarre or impossible situations without the movie stopping to explain what’s happening.

Examples of the feeling I’m looking for: **The Exterminating Angel (1962), Beau Is Afraid (2023), and After Hours (1985)** — although they all do it in very different ways.

I’m especially interested in lesser-known movies where you eventually realize: **“Wait… when did this stop being normal?”**

Any recommendations?

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I’m Thinking of Ending Things
2. The Devils Advocate  
American Psycho  
Mother  
A Different Man
  - Mother’s a great answer for this.
3. Synecdoche, New York
4. Mulholland Drive (2001)

Being John Malkovich (1999)

Jacob's ladder (1990)
5. Brazil is the first one that came to mind.  It crosses the line from reality into madness, but although I have seen it a dozen times I can never really pinpoint where that happens! 
6. Barton Fink
7. Coherence
8. Donnie Darko (2001) - has a really cool & deep story that you’d be forgiven for not understanding until it’s all laid out in front of you
9. Vivarium (2019).  Creepy, absurd and unsettling.  I loved it.

8. Happy Death Day

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. This Is the End(2013) - directed by Seth Rogen & Evan Goldberg

**Score:** 1321
**Body:** This is genuinely one of the most cherished comedies for me. i’ve come back to it over the years and somehow appreciate it even more every time. it’s an easy 10/10 for me. what i love about it is how much it gets out of such a simple setup. the screenplay and the characters are doing almost all the work, and bcuz the movie is so meta and committed to its own weirdness, it’s just ridiculously fun. there are so many great character moments and these completely bizarre little adventures, but none of it feels like it needs some massive budget or endless CGI to work. and that’s what i really miss about movies like this. something made for around $50 million can still be this creative and this entertaining without having to turn everything into a giant spectacle. they just don’t make enough movies like this anymore.

and that Channing Tatum cameo is exactly the kind of cameo i want to see more of. he clearly had the balls to go completely crazy with it, and it makes the whole thing even funnier. i really want more movies that are willing to be this weird and just have fun with themselves. the only recent movie i can think of that even remotely gave me this feeling was The Naked Gun.

## 2. Wow. Just… Wow! So I just watched Disclosure Day (2026)

**Score:** 945
**Body:** This is without a doubt the worst movie ever made by Spielberg.

I am in disbelief how bad it was.

I guess he’s going soft in the head and no one has the guts to step in.

Where to even begin?

The bizarre and terrible acting?

The nonsensical blocking?

The glacier pacing?

Or the most ridiculously up its own ass premise?

I think this may be the worst movie of the year.

I think it may be worse than The Happening.

My favorite scene was the guy sneaking up to a fence, then sneaking along it (which had no cover, mind you), and cutting to him sneaking up to the same fence a second time.

All while the police searching… A random ditch? Don’t turn around to look at the guy because reasons.

### Top 5 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Spielberg used his goodwill on this one . Next time I’ll be waiting for reviews before I blindly go in.
  - Same on trusting the name. But then critic and audience reviews were good! Everything about it, baffling
2. It was not what I was expecting, quality wise, at all. My favorite was hiding behind the fence before stealing the agents cars as well. Everything made less sense as it went on. 
  - The film made little sense when you realize that the whole premise of the film (95% of the action) consisted of getting some film to a TV station...

...when they had a live alien willing to go on camera.

Who the hell cares about old footage, some of which we might have seen before, when you have the real deal willing to grab a mike and say ***"Nanu Nanu"*** to the whole world.
    - THIS!!!! It’s 2026, just put everything on the internet and be done with it!!! 

To me, it just spoke volumes of Spielberg’s “boomer” tendencies…. Still thinking that the majority of people today get their news from 24/7 news channels… and that they NEEDED to put it all on the air. 
      - Like eeryone's gonna be stopped watching TVs in a display window right by a news stand 
  - There’s a moment like this in Aliens where Dietrich bends down slightly to lean into to a wall to look at something and then a different take of the same action is used again, this time to lift up a partially entombed colonist’s head. I never don’t notice it. It’s a pretty minor detail in a largely thrilling and rightly lauded film, however; Disclosure Day being neither of these
  - Pretty woeful movie.

What I did like was Colin Firth and his character. He’s the main antagonist throughout maybe the first 2/3rds of the film but for a significant chunk near the end he’s like, sitting in a chair with a dumbfounded look his face. Also kind of a look of amazement. I wish they would have gone to that more in general. 

It was just interesting seeing that approach, usually that sort of character is full-on to the end, so it was neat to watch Firth do that, and he’s a very good actor so his face told the story. Rest of the movie lost me.
3. "This is going to change everything" "This changes everything" "Everything is going to change" 

I feel like there was some variation on that slop statement every 10 minutes. 


4. I think I would have enjoyed it had I not felt completely bamboozled by the marketing. I was there to see what was disclosed and what happened after. Instead we got a fairly middling story about running from the government.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. The Remains of the Day is one of the greatest adaptations ever

**Score:** 114
**Body:** Conversations about book to film adaptations tend to focus on length and often turn into checklists going over how many of the source material’s plot points are pasted into the final movie. Categorizing art forms primarily by such superficial characteristics as duration is reductive and revealing of someone who has failed to engage with a medium beyond its surface and thereby missed what makes the medium unique. *The Remains of the Day* is an excellent adaptation in every respect, that uses the language of cinema to convey the ideas, themes, and motifs of its source material without feeling encumbered by it. 

Kazuo Ishiguro’s original novel is particularly difficult to adapt on the surface. So much of the book centres around Stevens’ reflections and recollections which Ishiguro presents using Stevens’ inner voice. One of the main strengths of the novel is Ishiguro’s delicate and skillful (well most of the time anyway but this isn’t a book review) weaving of Stevens’ interiority, such that translating this to the screen where the means of freely depicting such an inner voice are far more limited, is exceptionally difficult. 

This meticulous fleshing out of Stevens’ character through his inner monologue also serves to establish his relationship with the reader as one of Ishiguro’s primary aims with *The Remains of the Day* was to communicate the idea that we are all butlers, in one way or another and in a connected world we can only hope that our service to whatever it is we serve might bring about something positive in spite of our powerlessness. This is also what led him to conceive of the idea of using a butler as his main character. His outlook is perhaps more liberal than my tastes permit but it remains an idea worth exploring and the relationship is successfully developed. Thus, the film’s challenge is not merely to flesh Stevens out but also to carry onto the screen the relationship Ishiguro managed to craft with the reader. 

The film overcomes these challenges and succeeds as an adaptation for two primary reasons. The first is Anthony Hopkins’ performance as Stevens. Anyone who knows me knows I don’t discuss performances much when talking about movies because I find them a lazy way to praise a film without engaging with anything substantial. Nevertheless, this is a case where the lead actor’s performance is one of the driving forces behind the film’s success and without it, the translation of Stevens’ inner voice into the cinema, would not have been possible. One cannot help but marvel at the care and depth with which Hopkins embodies Stevens in every frame in which he appears. Stevens is a character whose defining characteristic is suppression. Hopkins therefore has to make **non-expression***** *****expressive**. His pauses, posture, microscopic changes in facial expression, manner of speaking, and physical distance from others, all become substitutes for the enormous amount of psychological information Ishiguro can simply give us through prose.

The second way the film succeeds is through subtle choices by which Stevens’ inner thoughts from the book are conveyed through dialogue or interactions with other characters. This is a delicate challenge since done without precision, it can easily appear clumsy. But the filmmakers do so at precisely the right moments and in precisely the right ways. One example from the book is a story Stevens recounts that he once heard from his father who was also a butler. About an English butler in India who once encountered a tiger beneath his master’s dining table, calmly shot it, wiped off the remains, and served dinner as usual. This is an important story because it serves several purposes such as highlighting the relationship between Stevens and his father, as well as his worldview and sense of duty which Ishiguro interrogates throughout the novel, until the very end when it begins to crack under the weight of a lifetime of regret and experience. 

To tell the same story, the film has Stevens’ father recount it to the rest of the staff in Stevens’ presence while making clear that Stevens has heard it before and nods along approvingly. This establishes that the story is already part of Stevens’ understanding of himself while preserving everything else the story conveys in the novel. It is choices like this the film makes that appear to be small but are quite incredible. 

The film is also well made and pretty to look at in a functional, fully immersive sense rather than a “look at me I’m supposed to be a gorgeous period drama” sense that many period films adopt and I find the former far more respectable.

Check out my Letterboxd to keep up with what I watch and write. It’s aliasad. Or click on the link to go to the review and my profile.

https://boxd.it/g6bgtR

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I appreciate your thoughtful remarks on this film, which I love.  I've always admired the way that the movie touches on the lives of other characters, such as the optimistic young staff members who want to marry and move on and out into the world (in contrast to Stevens, who allows his chance at happiness to pass by) and also the portrayal of his father whose advanced age has rendered him incapable of any longer performing the household role which his entire identity and self-respect depend on.  I agree with you that Mr. Hopkins gives a nuanced performance that largely carries the film and is crucial to its achievement.
2. I’ve always felt if the film used the inner monologue style that Ishiguro uses throughout the novel, it would have been too expository and remove the sense of longing you feel when reading the novel. The change to use silence and emotional expression (largely due to Hopkins as you said) made it perfect for the medium.

It remains my favourite novel of all time, great review
3. One of my favorite books, I've long put off watching the film because of skepticism of how the book could translate to screen, even having heard how well the movie was received.
May have to finally watch it this week.
  - Understandable.

It's the other way around for me. I adore the film; I don't think I could read the book without the memory of the film interfering.

Tried it once before: loved the adaptation of The English Patient; it was impossible to read the novel afterwards.
    - Personally, if I love the literary source for a film I never see the movie.  I was blown away by the novel **The French Lieutenant's Woman** (1969) and severely disappointed by the film version released in 1981.  It managed to drain away all the wit and sophistication of the book.  It boasted a great director, a screenplay by Harold Pinter, and starred Meryl Streep & Jeremy Irons - as the old Hollywood saying goes, 'It takes an incredible amount of talent to make a movie this bad'.
  - *Never Let Me Go* is my favorite book, but I also loved *The Remains of the Day*. I have seen both movie adaptations.

Now, IMO, as film is a different medium than the written word, I don't think a successful adaptation should try tell the exact same story as the source material in the exact same way. The different media each have their own strengths and weaknesses that the story should play itself to. So I always try to go into movie adaptations with an open mind and not sit there looking for differences to critique.

That said, *The Remains of the Day* is absolutely my favorite adaptation and, as I recall, it tells the exact same story. The movie enhances the book and vice-versa. This is all the more extraordinary because what I love about Ishiguro is his lyrical melancholy writing as much as the story itself. With *The Remains of the Day*, the movie really does a terrific job of capturing the mood of the book.

Conversely, the movie adaptation of *Never Let Me Go* was an utter disappointment for me. This may simply be a story that doesn't adapt itself to film well though. I am similarly not too hopeful about the upcoming *Klara and the Sun* movie either. Really enjoyed the book, but really not sure how Klara's inner monologue is going to adapt and I'm not a fan Taika Waititi, so that pessimism will be hard for me to overlook.

This is all to say: I would be surprised if a reader of *The Remains of the Day* didn't enjoy the film too. And FWIW, my spouse enjoyed neither the book nor the film (and is not a fan of Ishiguro in general; yet we remain married).
  - The film is a genuine masterpiece. I’ve rewatched it too many times to count. It’s flawless from start to finish. Of course, like all great art, it transcends the direct subject to ask of each of us: *for whom do you subordinate yourself - and at what cost.*

The next to last scene, of the bus departing in the rain, echoes for so many of us who have made irredeemable errors in love. Heartbreak and then some.
4. I love the book and the film adaptation. For me, the image of the late afternoon light entering the windows of the manor house and highlighting the dust of the empty rooms perfectly captures the tone and psychology of the book. The sense of loss, grief, and regret is so palpable in that one choice. It told the story in a single visual, which is what truly great directors do. 

Another one of my fave adaptations is the Merchant Ivory masterpiece A Room With A View. Utterly perfect.

## 3. James Gray’s We Own the Night is severely underrated

**Score:** 22
**Body:** If you think The Godfather is a masterpiece, and I’m pretty confident most people do, then you should absolutely love James Gray’s We Own the Night. 

This film explores devotion to family and morality and personal ethics in much the same way as The Godfather. Joaquin Phoenix’s character arc is the inverse of Michael Corleono’s arc. He starts in a criminal underworld and his family pulls him into law enforcement, and the incredible thing is that it ends with the same melancholy that the Godfather reserves for Michael becoming the head of a crime family. 

James Gray’s first three films are all incredibley Coppola-esque but We Own the Night is the best of the bunch. I’m fascinated by its tepid response when it came out so hope it gets a reappraisal. 

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. His whole filmography is underrated by wide swaths of cinema culture — with the notable exception of some French critics who seemed to always have understood the depth and quality of his work. 

His previous crime films, “We Own the Night” and “The Yards” especially, are some of my favorite films of his oeuvre, so I’m really looking forward to his latest one, “Paper Tiger,” since it sounds like it’s in a similar vein.
  - Lost City of Z is a fucking great movie
    - Absolutely love that film! The wife’s letter that she narrates is sooooooo powerful.

Also a great performance from Charlie Hunnam it has to be said
  - If James Gray is making a movie about the Russian mafia in Brighton beach I will be seated 
  - He has a Claire Denis vibe for sure. His style reminds me of White Material. 
2. I got really into Grey because Criterion featured several of his movies on their streamer. I was hooked after Little Odessa. He has a beautiful and slow storytelling style that I find mesmerizing, and I think it says a lot that actors clearly love to work with him. His exploration of the male psychology is so compelling and sensitive.

This describes why I have a tepid response to James Gray's films. To me, they feel like pastiches of 70s New Hollywood cinema rather than something original. 

## 4. You Were Never Really Here (2017)

**Body:** I just finished watching this film, and I’m honestly struggling to understand what I’m supposed to take away from it.

I know the movie is intentionally ambiguous, but I feel like I’m missing something important, especially when it comes to the ending and the main character’s motivations.

For those who enjoyed or understood the film better than I did: what do you think the movie was ultimately trying to say? And how do you interpret the ending?

I’d genuinely like to hear different interpretations because I feel like there’s probably more going on beneath the surface than I picked up on.

### Top 2 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

With that said, I feel like if the viewer has seen Taxi Driver (and the dozens of Taxi Driver inspired films since then) you can see the template YWNRH is following and therefore it allows you to focus more on Ramsay's particular style and interests, which is in line with her other films. I see it as a character study on depression and self-loathing.
